# 👓 Conceptual review

# **Foundation PRD — Conceptual Review & Observations**

Reference: [Foundation PRDs (Google Doc)](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1PFxKLHstI1tVcyJ-TA9aPOOnciwogCwgS25B7-7NNmY/edit?pli=1&tab=t.x7gws7e1jlhu)

> **Note on numbering:** This document was generated and revised over multiple sessions. Items were added, removed and restructured throughout. As a result, some identifiers in each section (C-1, T-4, etc.) may be absent from the sequence — this is intentional, not an error. All identifiers should be treated as unique reference labels, not sequential indices. Use them to cite or respond to a specific point.

---

## **Document Structure**

The Foundation PRDs comprise five interrelated documents:

| Document | Title | Status |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Document 0 | Business Logic Decisions Record | Locked — Source of truth |
| PRD 1 | Business Registration & Onboarding | Draft — Internal EPD Review |
| PRD 2 | Counterparty Management | Draft — Internal EPD Review |
| PRD 3 | Admin Verification Interface | Draft — Internal EPD Review |
| Roles & Permissions PRD | Roles, Permissions & Access Architecture | Draft — Internal EPD Review |

---

## **What the PRD Is About**

The Foundation PRDs define the **core identity and access infrastructure** for the QAWAFEL APEX platform before any transaction, invoice, or payment can occur. The platform needs to know who businesses are, how verified they are and what they are permitted to do. These documents establish those rules.

### The Central Mechanism: Three-Tier Progressive Verification

Everything in the Foundation PRDs is structured to enforce a tier model where admin approval of independent sections unlocks platform capabilities progressively — not all-or-nothing.

| Tier | Admin Approval Trigger | Capabilities Unlocked |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Tier 1 | Section 1 — Core Business Identification (CR confirmed) | Appear as Platform Verified to counterparties. Add counterparties. Import/view invoices. |
| Tier 2 | Section 2 — Beneficial Owners (identity confirmed) | Full commercial operations: issue invoices, payment links, ZATCA submission, invoice financing, receive payments. |
| Tier 3 | Section 3 — Bank Account (IBAN approved) | Settlement payouts to bank account. |

Source: Document 0, Section 2 "Admin Verification & Progressive Access" and Section 4 "Progressive Access Matrix."

### What It Addresses

**PRD 1 — Business Registration & Onboarding** Covers sign-up (email \+ password), a four-step onboarding wizard (Account Creator Details, Core Business Identification, Beneficial Owners, Bank Account Details), the role declaration at Step 1 that determines whether an ownership invitation is required, Save & Continue Later behaviour, multi-business login and entity selection, dashboard states per tier and the re-submission flow when admin rejects fields.

**PRD 2 — Counterparty Management** Covers how verified businesses manage their trading partners across three creation paths: Path A (manual CR-first entry), Path B (automatic extraction from ZATCA invoice import) and Path C (contact enrichment via API or bulk CSV upload). Also covers the badge model (Unverified / Platform Verified), internal quality labels, automatic silent merge when a counterparty self-registers and reaches Tier 1 and the payment link sharing flow when contact fields are missing.

**PRD 3 — Admin Verification Interface** Covers the Qawafel Operations team's tools for reviewing business submissions — the pending verification queue, field-level approve/reject with per-section tier unlocking, the CR cross-reference step against MoC, IBAN mathematical validation display, re-submission handling, ownership invitation monitoring and the all-businesses canonical directory showing both registered businesses and counterparty records.

**Roles & Permissions PRD** Covers the permission engine architecture, role definitions (Owner, Admin; Finance deferred), the Authorized Signatory flag as an orthogonal boolean, Qawafel internal admin roles (Super Admin, Operations, Support, Finance/Settlement, Risk & Compliance) and the permission matrices for both business users and Qawafel staff. Explicitly structured in two layers: Layer 1 (locked surfaces, buildable now) and Layer 2 (deferred until corresponding PRDs are locked).

**Document 0 — Business Logic Decisions Record** The shared foundation. Defines the tier model, ZATCA's role as a format validator (not an existence validator), the two external badge states, three internal quality labels, the counterparty merge trigger and scope, transaction permission rules and the field-level verification matrix. Downstream PRDs point back to this document rather than re-explaining the business logic.

---

## **Conflations**

Conflations are places where two distinct concepts are being treated as the same thing, creating ambiguity that may surface as bugs or misaligned implementations.

---

### C-2. "Counterparty" as a Term Conflates Three Distinct Concepts

**Where it appears:**

The word "counterparty" is used throughout the Foundation PRDs to mean three different things and the distinction is not made explicit.

**Concept 1 — The Business (entity)** Any company or freelancer that has a presence on the platform — either because they self-registered or because another business added them as a trading partner.

**Concept 2 — The Trading Partner Relationship** The relationship between two businesses — that Business XYZ has added Business ABC to their network and trades with them.

The PRDs often describe this through a "counterparty record" that appears to belong to the adding business. That is the clearest textual signal that the entity and the relationship are being blurred together.

**Concept 3 — The Transactional Role** "The other party" to a specific invoice, payment link, or financing interaction.

**Useful working distinction:**

- **Registered Business** — has an APEX account, went through onboarding, and may hold verification tiers depending on admin approval.  
- **Unregistered Business** — appears on the platform because another business added it as a trading partner, but has no APEX account and no verification tiers. In practice it may begin with only partial identity/contact data.

The ambiguity matters because the PRDs sometimes use "counterparty" as though it were a different class of entity from a business, and at other times as shorthand for either the relationship or the transactional role. That can lead Product, Design, and Engineering to reason about badges, directories, and merge rules differently.

The most revealing symptom is this phrase pattern, which appears across Document 0 and PRD 2:

Document 0, Section "Counterparty Addition & Minimum Data":

> "When a counterparty self-registers and reaches Tier 1..."

PRD 2, Section 7, FR-D.1:

> "When a business reaches Tier 1 the platform runs an exact CR/UNN match against all counterparty records platform-wide."

This creates a semantic inconsistency. A business added by another merchant does not become a different kind of thing when it later registers on APEX; what changes is its registration and verification state.

The badge model inherits the same problem directly:

Document 0, Section 5:

> "Badge (external): **Unverified** — counterparty has no self-registered business with matching CR." "Badge (external): **Platform Verified** — counterparty self-registered and reached Tier 1."

What the badge is actually describing is: *is the Business in your network registered and verified on APEX?* The badge reads more naturally as a property of the business entity, surfaced through the trading partner relationship.

**Recommended terminology cleanup:**

The term "counterparty" is appropriate in exactly one context: the transactional role. "The counterparty on this invoice" (the other party to a specific document), or "counterparty risk" in a financing context, are legitimate uses. The term should be retired from all entity and record contexts and replaced as follows:

| Current PRD language | Should be |
| :---- | :---- |
| PRD 2 title: "Counterparty Management" | "Trading Partner Management" |
| "counterparty record" (when meaning the entity) | "Business record" |
| "counterparty directory" | "Business network" |
| "counterparty profile" | "Business profile" |
| "Add Counterparty form" | "Add Business" |
| "Unverified counterparty" (badge state) | "Unverified Business" |
| "Platform Verified counterparty" (badge state) | "Platform Verified Business" |
| "when a counterparty self-registers" | "when the Business registers" |
| Document 0 "Counterparty Addition & Minimum Data" | "Business Addition & Minimum Data" |
| PRD 3 All-Businesses Directory: "counterparty records (CP)" | "Unregistered Business records" |
| "network directory" (Q4 deferred search feature) | "Business Directory" |

**Business Network vs Business Directory — a necessary distinction:**

These are two separate concepts that must not be conflated:

- **Business Network** — a business's own scoped collection of trading partners. Built through Path A (manual addition), Path B (ZATCA invoice import), or Path C (bulk upload / API). Every business on the platform has their own network. An Unregistered Business in XYZ's network is a canonical Business record linked to XYZ through a trading partner relationship.  
    
- **Business Directory** — a platform-wide searchable listing of all registered businesses on APEX. A Q4 deferred feature that allows a business to search for and discover other platform businesses by trade name, without needing to know their CR number. When a match is found, that Business can be added directly to the searching business's network. The Business Directory is the discovery layer that feeds into the Business Network.

**Impact:** This is first a terminology problem and only secondarily a modelling problem. Even if Product keeps the current merge model, the language should still be tightened so that "counterparty" is used for the transactional role and the entity/relationship concepts are named explicitly.

---

### C-3. Counterparty Records as Copies vs. References — Major Architectural Assumption Hidden in the PRD

**Where it appears:**

Document 0, Section "Counterparty Addition & Minimum Data":

> "Merge trigger: Silent, automatic, exact CR match only. When a counterparty self-registers and reaches Tier 1 (CR confirmed by admin), the platform performs an exact CR match against existing counterparty records. If match found, full overwrite of counterparty record fields with verified data."

PRD 2, Section 7 "Automatic Merge on Self-Registration," FR-D.2:

> "For each counterparty record where the CR/UNN matches exactly, the platform performs a full overwrite of record fields with the self-registered business's verified data."

The current wording appears to assume a copy-and-merge model: business data is stored in network-scoped records and later overwritten when a self-registered business reaches Tier 1\. That may be the intended product model, but it is not surfaced as an explicit design decision with its consequences.

**Impact:** If Product intends a copy-and-merge model, the PRD should explicitly own the consequences: duplicate detection, survivor rules, overwrite scope, transaction reassignment, auditability, and ops remediation. If Product intends a more canonical-record model, the merge section will likely simplify. The key issue is not that one model is inherently wrong; it is that the model choice is currently implicit while many downstream rules depend on it.

---

### C-4. TIN and VAT Registration Number Treated as a Single Field in PRD 2

**Where it appears:**

PRD 2, Section 2.1 "Counterparty Profile Fields" lists:

> "VAT registration number (TIN) | Number | Optional | Secondary matching key. Extracted from ZATCA invoice buyer TIN for Path B. Absent for non-taxable counterparties."

These are treated as a single combined field with a single label. But Document 0 and PRD 1 treat them as two distinct fields:

PRD 1, FR-3.3:

> "required fields for Business type are CR or Unified number... TIN (10 digits)... VAT Registration Number (15-digit, starting and ending with 3\) and VAT Certificate upload are shown only if the business selects VAT registered."

Document 0, Field-Level Verification Matrix (Section 6\) lists them as separate rows:

> "Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN) — 10-digit (businesses) or 12-digit (individuals)." "VAT Registration Number — 15-digit starting and ending with 3\. Only shown if business is VAT-registered."

**Impact:** The Business record data model in PRD 2 would have an ambiguous field that does not cleanly map to either the onboarding data model or the admin review model. ZATCA matching logic that uses TIN as a secondary key (PRD 2, FR-B.1) may operate on an incorrect field if TIN and VAT number are conflated in the Business record.

---

### C-5. The "Non-Taxable Toggle" Is Named Backwards

**Where it appears:**

PRD 1, FR-3.2:

> "A non-taxable toggle is shown prominently in Step 2\. When switched off, the platform shows a warning before confirming: 'Declaring your business as non-taxable means VAT invoicing and ZATCA submission will not be available on APEX. This declaration cannot be changed without contacting support.' The user must confirm to proceed." "Toggle on by default."

Reading FR-3.2 literally: the toggle is labelled "non-taxable," it is **On** by default and it is turned **Off** to declare non-taxable status. In standard UX convention, a toggle labelled "non-taxable" that is **On** means the business IS non-taxable. But the PRD intends the opposite: **On \= taxable (normal state), Off \= non-taxable declaration**.

FR-3.3 confirms the confusion: it is titled "When the non-taxable toggle is On (default):" and then describes the taxable business fields. The toggle is functionally a "taxable toggle," not a "non-taxable toggle."

FR-3.4: "When the non-taxable toggle is Off: TIN, VAT Registration Number and VAT Certificate upload fields are hidden from Step 2."

**Impact:** The toggle name, direction and default could lead to a different implementation than intended if taken literally. A developer reading "non-taxable toggle is On by default" could implement the platform treating all businesses as non-taxable by default — the opposite of the intended behaviour.

---

### C-6. "Approve Business" CTA Conflated with Progressive Tier Unlocking

**Where it appears:**

PRD 3, Section 4.3 "Tier Unlock Mechanics," FR-R.1:

> "Approving all actionable fields in Tab 1 (Core Business Identification) immediately unlocks Tier 1 for the business."

PRD 3, Section 4.5 "Finalising the Review," FR-R.14:

> "The Approve Business CTA is available only when all actionable fields in each Tab have been approved."

PRD 3, FR-R.16:

> "Clicking Approve Business sends the appropriate tier notifications and moves the business to the correct Active status."

The PRD describes two simultaneously active models: (1) tiers unlock **immediately and automatically** as each section's fields are fully approved and (2) a final "Approve Business" CTA is required to conclude the review. These coexist without explicit reconciliation. If Tier 1 already unlocked when Section 1 was approved and Tier 2 already unlocked when Section 2 was approved, what does "Approve Business" do that has not already happened?

**Impact:** If "Approve Business" is just an administrative finalisation step (removes the business from the queue, marks it "Active" in the directory), that needs to be made explicit. If missing the CTA leaves tiers unlocked but the business in a limbo status, that scenario would benefit from explicit resolution before implementation.

---

## **Tensions and Challenges**

Tensions are places where two legitimate requirements pull in opposite directions, or where a product decision creates implementation difficulty that has not been acknowledged.

---

### T-1. Clean Slate Rule vs. Pre-Existing Transaction History

**Where it appears:**

Document 0, Section "Counterparty Data Merging & Pre-onboarding Transactions":

> "Newly onboarded business view: Clean slate. A business that self-registers sees no pre-existing transactions recorded by other businesses against them."

PRD 2, FR-D.6:

> "The newly self-registered business sees no pre-existing transactions recorded by other businesses against them. They arrive on a clean slate."

**The tension:** The privacy rationale is sound — business A should not see what business C privately recorded about them. But as written, the rule also hides the business's own prior interactions. A business may have been the buyer on multiple payment links generated by other platform users before registering. Seeing none of that history on first login may feel unexpected and could reduce trust.

PRD 2, FR-D.7 adds a partial carve-out:

> "The newly self-registered business can see their own imported documents — invoices they imported via API or bulk upload."

This only covers invoices the business themselves imported, not payments they made through other sellers' links. The carve-out is inconsistently scoped.

**Recommendation:** Consider offering newly registered businesses an opt-in to surface their pre-existing transaction history — specifically, transactions where they were the buyer or counterparty on a payment link or invoice generated by another platform business. This is distinct from seeing another business's private records about them: the scope is limited to transactions they were directly a party to. An opt-in (rather than automatic surfacing) preserves the clean-slate default while giving businesses who want visibility the ability to access their own history. This resolves the tension without compromising the privacy principle.

This is a product recommendation, not a blocker in the current PRD.

---

### T-2. Path A Badge vs. Platform Verified Status for Already-Registered Businesses

**Where it appears:**

PRD 2, FR-A.3:

> "The system checks whether a business on the platform has the same CR/UNN — meaning the counterparty is already registered on APEX. If yes the platform pre-populates available verified fields. User sees: 'This business is registered on APEX. Their verified details have been pre-filled.'"

PRD 2, FR-A.4 (immediately following):

> "On save the counterparty record is created with Unverified badge and 'Manually Entered' internal quality label."

So when Path A detects a Tier 1+ registered business and pre-populates their verified fields, the resulting Business record is still created with an **Unverified badge**. But compare to Path B:

PRD 2, FR-B.6:

> "If a Path B extracted CR/UNN matches a currently registered and Tier 1+ platform business, the counterparty record is immediately upgraded to Platform Verified and the linked platform account field is populated."

Path A and Path B have **different outcomes for the same Business state**. If the Business is already Tier 1+ on the platform, Path B gives Platform Verified immediately; Path A gives Unverified.

**Impact:** The badge model would behave differently depending on how the Business was added to the network, despite pointing at the same registered Business.

---

### T-3. Full Onboarding Submission Delays Progressive Review

**Where it appears:**

PRD 1, Section 4 introduction:

> "Steps 3 and 4 can be saved and completed later."

PRD 1, FR-2.5:

> "The Submit for Review CTA is available only when all required fields across all four steps are complete."

PRD 3, Section 4.3 "Tier Unlock Mechanics," FR-R.1:

> "Approving all actionable fields in Tab 1 (Core Business Identification) immediately unlocks Tier 1 for the business."

**The tension:** The documents are internally consistent: admin unlocks tiers progressively after review starts, but the business cannot enter review until all required fields across all four onboarding steps are complete. This means Tier 1 review cannot begin while Step 4 (bank details) is still outstanding, even though bank approval is logically independent and only gates Tier 3\.

**Recommendation:** Product should confirm whether this delay is intentional. If yes, the PRD should state clearly that progressive unlocking happens only after full onboarding submission. If no, the onboarding PRD will need partial submission rules for Section 1, Section 2, and Section 3\.

---

### T-5. Tier Drop on Rejection — Cascading Effects Are Undefined

**Where it appears:**

PRD 3, Section 2 "Business Status Model (Admin View)":

> "Tier drop on rejection: if a business is at Tier 1 and the admin rejects a Section 1 field, the business drops below Tier 1 until the field is re-approved. If a business is at Tier 2 and a Section 2 field is rejected, the business drops below Tier 2\. Tier 1 is preserved when only Section 2 fields are rejected."

The PRD defines the tier drop rule but is entirely silent on its downstream effects:

- Businesses in other businesses' networks that have this business marked as "Platform Verified" (set on the Tier 1 merge trigger): do they revert to Unverified on a tier drop?  
- Other businesses that have already generated invoices or payment links against this business as a "Platform Verified" Business: what status do those documents show?  
- If a Tier 2 business drops to Tier 1 because a Section 2 field is rejected, Tier 2-gated operations (payment links, invoice issuance) become blocked — but what happens to active payment links already generated under Tier 2?

None of these cascading effects are addressed anywhere in the PRDs. Document 0's transaction permissions matrix (Section 3\) defines what is permitted at each tier, but not what happens to already-permitted transactions when a tier is revoked.

---

### T-6. Business Email Is the Registrant's Personal Work Email

**Where it appears:**

PRD 1, FR-AC.2:

> "Required fields collected in Step 1: Full Name, Work Email, Mobile Number, Designation."

PRD 1, FR-1.2:

> "Email address must be unique across all APEX accounts."

The "Work Email" collected in Step 1 becomes the unique identifier for the user's APEX account and the notification address for the business. Verification confirmations, tier unlock notifications, rejection alerts and ownership invitations all go to this address.

**The tension:** There is no "business email" concept in the platform. The registrant's personal work email becomes the business communication channel. If the registrant is removed from the organisation, their personal email remains the notification address for the business indefinitely. There is no mechanism defined for updating the primary notification email without it being tied to the personal account.

---

### T-7. Multi-Business Switching Requires Logout

**Where it appears:**

PRD 1, FR-8.5:

> "The user can switch between businesses by logging out."

PRD 1, Section 2 "User Types":

> "Multi-Business User: A user who is a member of more than one business on APEX. At login they see a business selection screen and choose which business context to enter. They can switch between businesses. This requires log out and login again."

**The tension:** The Multi-Business User is defined as a first-class user type, but the switching experience — a full logout to change business context — is at odds with that. The business selection screen already exists at login and presents a clean mental model for context switching. Requiring a logout to re-trigger it adds friction where none is architecturally necessary.

**Recommendation:** Consider extending the business selection screen into an active context-switching surface — accessible in-session from the navigation (e.g. a business switcher in the top bar), not only at login. The user experience at login and the mid-session switch could share the same screen. This keeps the model simple: one selection screen, usable both at login and whenever the user wants to change context. No logout required.

**Note on `active_merchant_id`:** The Roles PRD, Section 10 "Non-Functional Requirements" references `active_merchant_id` by name as an internal session field. This is an implementation detail — a specific field name — that has no place in a PRD. The product intent (all actions are scoped to the active business context; cross-business data must not leak) is valid and belongs in a PRD. The specific mechanism for enforcing it does not. This is one of several instances of implementation language in the PRDs covered in the separate section below.

This is a UX recommendation rather than a blocking inconsistency.

---

### T-8. IBAN Mathematical Validation vs. Admin Approval Action

**Where it appears:**

PRD 3, FR-R.12:

> "For the IBAN field the review view shows the system's mathematical validation result (Valid / Invalid — format and checksum) before the admin makes their approve or reject decision."

Document 0, Section 6 "Field-Level Verification Matrix":

> "IBAN: System performs mathematical IBAN validation (format and checksum). Result shown to admin before decision. Approving IBAN implicitly validates Bank Name since it is derived from the IBAN."

**The tension:** If the system validates IBAN format and checksum mathematically, the admin's action adds no independent verification — they are being asked to approve or reject something the system has already assessed objectively. Can an admin approve an IBAN the system has flagged as Invalid? Can they reject one the system has flagged as Valid? The PRD shows the result to the admin but does not define whether this result is a hard gate or purely advisory. If it is advisory, an IBAN the system has flagged as Invalid could be approved. If it is a hard gate, the admin action is a redundant UX step.

---

### T-9. Auto-Save Behaviour — Permanent vs. Session

**Where it appears:**

PRD 1, FR-2.3:

> "Steps 3 and 4 can be partially completed and saved for later via Save & Continue Later. When the user saves mid-wizard and navigates away, a resume banner appears on the Dashboard."

PRD 1, FR-2.4:

> "All form fields auto-save on blur. Save & Continue Later immediately persists all current field values. If the user closes the browser mid-wizard all fields entered are present when they return."

FR-2.4 says "closes the browser" and fields persist on return — which implies permanent server-side persistence. But "auto-save on blur" is often implemented as browser-local state (localStorage/sessionStorage). The distinction matters: server-side persistence means every field blur triggers a persistence event for a half-completed wizard, including for users who will never return. Session storage means cross-device continuation is not supported. This is a meaningful architectural choice that requires explicit resolution before the onboarding wizard is built.

---

## **Gaps and Misses**

Gaps are requirements, decisions, or flows that are referenced but not specified, or entirely absent despite being necessary for a complete implementation.

---

### G-1. Duplicate FR-R.19 in PRD 3

**Where it appears:**

PRD 3, Section 4.4 "Field-Level Review Actions," FR-R.19:

> "Admin can unlock a field to re-review it after submission and the same verification process applies. An alert banner should appear to notify the admin that unlock the fields will send the application back to verification process."

PRD 3, Section 4.6 "Re-submission Handling," FR-R.19:

> "When a business re-submits after a rejection the review view shows a re-submission banner with the attempt number and highlights only the re-submitted (previously rejected) fields for review."

Two separate functional requirements share the same ID. One of them is unnumbered and untraceable. The requirement in Section 4.6 that should follow FR-R.19 likely starts at FR-R.20 (which does exist), suggesting the Section 4.4 FR-R.19 was inserted late and renumbering was not applied. Given that PRD 3 was updated in v1.1, this is likely a continuity error from that revision.

---

### G-2. Document 0 Version Mismatch

**Where it appears:**

Document 0 header:

> "Version 1.1 | Status: Locked — Source of truth for all downstream PRDs"

Document 0 footer:

> "Document 0 — Business Logic Decisions Record | QAWAFEL APEX PLATFORM | Version 1.0"

The document that is the locked source of truth for all downstream PRDs has a version inconsistency between its header and footer. This is the document engineering teams are told to read before reading any PRD. The version ambiguity is minor in isolation but matters when decisions are attributed to "Document 0 v1.1."

---

### G-3. Path C Business Creation — Quality Label Is Undefined

**Where it appears:**

PRD 2, FR-C.5:

> "Three label values: Manually Entered (Path A creation), ZATCA Referenced Single Seller (Path B — one enrolled seller), ZATCA Referenced Multiple Sellers (Path B — two or more distinct enrolled sellers). Path C does not change the quality label."

PRD 2, Section 5.1 "Why Path C Exists":

> "Path C provides a scalable equivalent: sellers can supply a structured file or API payload containing buyer business identity and contact data and the platform handles record creation and enrichment automatically."

PRD 2, FR-G.2 (creation mode):

> "If no match is found and a CR/UNN number and Arabic legal name are both present, creation mode applies and a new counterparty record is created."

Path C can create new Business records in creation mode. But FR-C.5 says "Path C does not change the quality label" and the only three label values cover Path A and Path B. There is no quality label defined for a record created via Path C.

**Impact:** Every Path C-created Business record will have a null or undefined internal quality label. Since these labels feed "matching confidence scoring and future financing eligibility logic" (Document 0, Section 5), a null label on a Path C-created record may produce undefined behaviour in those downstream systems.

---

### G-4. Ownership Invitation — New User Account Creation Flow Is TBD

**Where it appears:**

PRD 1, FR-7.3:

> "The invitation email contains a unique one-time link expiring after 72 hours. The link directs the recipient to create an APEX account (if new: Logic TBD) or log in (if existing), after which the Owner role is assigned to their account for this business."

PRD 1, FR-7.5 (marked "Deferred"):

> "The Admin can resend an expired invitation from business settings. Resending generates a new 72-hour link and invalidates the previous one. (Logic TBD)"

PRD 1, FR-7.6 (marked "Deferred"):

> "The Admin can update the owner email address and resend. The previous invitation to the old email is invalidated. (Logic TBD)"

The ownership invitation flow is a first-class user journey for the authorized-registrant path, which represents a significant proportion of business registrations. When an invited owner who has no APEX account follows the link, the entire account creation flow is labelled "Logic TBD." Several questions remain open:

- Does the invited owner go through the full sign-up screen (email \+ password)?  
- Do they go through the onboarding wizard? If so, from which step?  
- What happens if they create an account with a different email than the one the invitation was sent to?  
- What fields does the system pre-populate for them?

Without this, the authorized-registrant path would be difficult to fully implement or test.

---

### G-5. Duplicate CR Registration — No Defined Behaviour

**Where it appears:**

PRD 1, FR-1.2:

> "Email address must be unique across all APEX accounts."

There is a uniqueness check on email at sign-up. There is no equivalent uniqueness check or defined behaviour for CR numbers at registration time.

The PRD has no FR addressing this case. A platform that uses CR as the primary identity anchor and bases its Business record merge logic on "exact CR match" has no specified behaviour when two separate registrations claim the same CR. This can occur legitimately (two authorised representatives of the same business both trying to register it) or fraudulently.

---

### G-6. Staff Invitation Flow — Referenced but Never Specified

**Where it appears:**

PRD 1, Section 10 "Out of Scope":

> "Staff invitation flow (inviting users beyond Owner) — defined in Roles & Permissions PRD."

Roles & Permissions PRD, Section 5 "Business User Permission Matrix," Layer 1:

> "Invite users | ✓ | ✓" (Owner and Admin can both do it)

The Roles & Permissions PRD lists "Invite users" as a permission in the matrix but provides no functional requirements, no FR IDs, no acceptance criteria and no UX description for how staff invitation actually works. The permission to invite users exists; the mechanism for doing so does not. PRD 1 defers to the Roles PRD; the Roles PRD does not deliver the specification.

**Impact:** User management — adding team members to a business account — is a core operational capability. It is listed in the permission matrix, but the implementable specification does not yet exist in any document.

---

### G-7. Freelancer Path Is Incompletely Specified Across All Three Business Addition Paths

**Where it appears:**

PRD 1, FR-3.1:

> "Business type selection — Business (Company) or Freelancer — is the first required field."

PRD 1, FR-3.5:

> "Required fields for Freelancer type: Freelance Certificate number, legal name in Arabic, Freelance Certificate upload, TIN (12 digits for individuals if taxable), national address."

PRD 2, Section 3.1, FR-A.1:

> "The Add Counterparty form requires: CR/UNN number or Freelance Certificate number and legal business name (Arabic)."

But Path B (FR-B.1) uses only CR/UNN and TIN/VAT as matching keys. Path C (FR-G.2) uses CR/UNN and Arabic legal name. Neither Path B nor Path C explicitly covers Freelance Certificate numbers as an anchor or matching key. The merge logic (FR-D.1, FR-D.2) references only "exact CR/UNN match."

**Impact:** If a freelancer self-registers, the automatic merge trigger uses "exact CR/UNN match" — but their anchor is a Freelance Certificate number, not a CR/UNN. The merge logic as specified would not trigger for freelancer Business records.

---

### G-8. VAT-Registered Declaration — No Form Step Defined

**Where it appears:**

PRD 1, FR-3.3:

> "VAT Registration Number (15-digit, starting and ending with 3\) and VAT Certificate upload are shown only if the business selects VAT registered."

There is no form element described — no checkbox, no radio button, no toggle — for the business to declare "I am VAT registered." The field is shown conditionally on this declaration, but how the declaration is made is undefined. The same FR says the non-taxable toggle controls TIN/VAT field visibility (toggle off hides TIN and VAT), but the VAT-registered sub-declaration (within taxable businesses) has no specified UI mechanism.

**Impact:** Without a specified mechanism, implementation would need to either add a UI element (such as a "VAT registered?" checkbox) or treat providing a VAT number as implicit declaration — the latter of which is a conditional field reveal rather than an explicit declaration.

---

### G-9. Non-Taxable Status Reversal — No Ops Workflow Defined

**Where it appears:**

PRD 1, FR-3.2:

> "This declaration cannot be changed without contacting support."

PRD 1, Open Question OQ-5:

> "If a non-taxable business later becomes VAT-registered (crossing the SAR 375,000 threshold), what is the process for updating their non-taxable declaration? This requires an ops workflow definition."

PRD 3, Open Question OQ-2:

> "If a business that declared non-taxable at onboarding later becomes VAT-registered, what is the admin process to update the declaration and add TIN and VAT fields to their record?"

The same gap is independently flagged in both PRD 1 and PRD 3\. The non-taxable declaration is presented as immutable without support, but no support workflow is defined. There are no FRs in any PRD covering:

- What fields are added to the business record when non-taxable is reversed  
- Whether a new admin review cycle is triggered  
- Whether Tier 1 needs to be re-earned  
- What happens to historical invoices issued under non-taxable status

This affects a likely operational scenario (businesses growing past the VAT threshold) and would benefit from a defined resolution path.

---

### G-10. Bank Account Update Post-Tier 3 — Review Cycle Undefined

**Where it appears:**

PRD 3, Open Question OQ-3:

> "If a business updates their bank account details post-approval (Tier 3 active), does the updated IBAN go through a full re-verification cycle before Tier 3 is re-granted, or is it an admin review of only the changed field?"

No FR in any PRD covers what happens when a Tier 3 business changes their bank account. Is Tier 3 immediately revoked on edit? Does it stay active while the new IBAN is under review? Can the business continue receiving settlement payouts to the old IBAN while the new one is being reviewed? These are operational certainties that have no specified behaviour.

---

### G-11. Inactive Account Expiry — No Policy Defined

**Where it appears:**

No FR in any PRD addresses account inactivity or expiry. The scenarios without defined behaviour include:

- Accounts created but never submitted for review  
- Accounts in "Action Required" state with no activity for an extended period  
- Whether an inactive registration "holds" the CR number, blocking others from registering the same business  
- Whether platform storage, queue slots, or session resources are ever reclaimed from abandoned registrations  
- Whether a tier drop combined with prolonged inactivity should be treated differently from a voluntary exit

For a platform where CR uniqueness is the identity anchor, an abandoned registration holding a CR number indefinitely could become a meaningful operational concern.

---

### G-12. Multiple Business Scenarios During Concurrent Registration — All Undefined

**Where it appears:**

PRD 2, Section 7 "Automatic Merge on Self-Registration" addresses only the case where a Business reaches Tier 1 as the trigger — it does not address what happens to Business records created while that business is in a pending or mid-registration state. Six concurrent registration scenarios have no defined behaviour:

1. Business ABC registers first (pending verification) and business XYZ tries to add ABC as a counterparty  
2. Business ABC registers first (verified) and business XYZ tries to add ABC as a counterparty  
3. Business XYZ manually added business ABC as a counterparty, then ABC tries to register  
4. Business XYZ ZATCA-imported business ABC as a counterparty, then ABC tries to register  
5. Multiple businesses manually added ABC as a counterparty, then ABC tries to register  
6. Multiple businesses ZATCA-imported ABC as a counterparty, then ABC tries to register

None of these scenarios are addressed in PRD 2\. Scenario 1 is the most immediately impactful: FR-A.3 says the form pre-populates with verified data if the CR matches a registered platform business — but a "pending verification" business has no verified data yet. What is pre-populated? What badge does the Business record get? Is the record linked to the pending business or not?

The merge logic in PRD 2 Section 7 addresses only "business reaches Tier 1" as the trigger — it does not address what happens to Business records created while that business is in the pending state.

---

### G-13. Path C Merge Rule Inconsistency with Document 0

**Where it appears:**

Document 0, Section "Counterparty Addition & Minimum Data":

> "Merge scope: Full overwrite with protection. Verified self-registered data overwrites all counterparty record fields."

PRD 2, Section 5.2 "Merge Logic for Path C Records":

> "Business identity fields (CR/UNN number, legal name in Arabic, TIN) follow the overwrite rule... Contact fields (email, phone) follow the gap-fill rule at all times, regardless of source. A contact field already present on a record is never overwritten by any subsequent Path C submission, Path B enrichment, or merge event."

PRD 2, Section 7 "Automatic Merge on Self-Registration," FR-D.2:

> "the platform performs a full overwrite of record fields with the self-registered business's verified data."

There is a direct conflict. Document 0 and FR-D.2 specify "full overwrite" for the merge. PRD 2 Section 5.2 carves out contact fields (email, phone) as gap-fill only, even on merge. Which rule governs when a self-registered business's merge event runs against a record that has contact data added by a seller via Path C?

If full overwrite applies, a seller's carefully maintained contact data for a Business is silently replaced the moment that Business self-registers. If the Path C gap-fill protection applies, the merge is not a full overwrite as Document 0 specifies. These two rules need reconciliation — the PRDs do not currently acknowledge the conflict.

## **Merge & Deduplication Brainstorming**

The merge section would benefit from explicit product thinking beyond the simple "exact CR match \-\> full overwrite" rule. Some of this will become engineering design, but the PRD still needs user-visible outcomes and business rules for the cases below.

Even if Product settles on a canonical Business model, these questions still exist — they simply become deduplication and record-consolidation rules rather than a classic "merge" event.

### M-1. Same CR/UNN, Different Trade Names

**Possible scenario:** Two records share the same CR/UNN but carry different Arabic or English names because one seller entered a trade name, another entered the legal name, or different sources supplied different labels.

**Questions to resolve:**

- Is exact CR/UNN alone sufficient to declare "same Business," even when names differ materially?  
- Which name is retained as the canonical display name after merge: verified legal name, latest source, or both with provenance?  
- Should losing names remain searchable as aliases?

### M-2. Same Business Created Twice Through Different Anchors

**Possible scenario:** Record A is created with CR/UNN and legal name. Record B is created separately with TIN and legal name or contact fields because the earlier flow had incomplete data and no shared anchor.

**Questions to resolve:**

- Under what conditions can CR/UNN and TIN be judged to represent the same Business before self-registration?  
- Is there a deterministic identifier hierarchy, for example: verified CR/UNN \> verified Freelance Certificate \> verified TIN \> seller-supplied TIN?  
- When confidence is not high enough, should the platform avoid auto-merge and instead create an ops review case?

### M-3. Duplicate Unregistered Records Already Referenced by Transactions

**Possible scenario:** Two Business records that later prove to be the same entity are already attached to invoices, payment links, financing invitations, or audit entries.

**Questions to resolve:**

- Do historical transactions get re-pointed to a survivor Business record, or do they continue referencing the original record while the directory view consolidates them?  
- If transactions are re-pointed, what immutable audit trail preserves the original linkage?  
- What should a merchant see on old documents after the deduplication event?

### M-4. Self-Registration After Multiple Partial Records Exist

**Possible scenario:** The same Business appears across multiple merchants' networks as several low-data records, then later self-registers and reaches Tier 1\.

**Questions to resolve:**

- Does the Tier 1 event attempt to merge only records with exact CR/UNN matches, or also candidate matches discovered through TIN or name heuristics?  
- If multiple candidate records exist, is there one survivor record platform-wide or one survivor per merchant network?  
- What is the expected user-visible result in each merchant directory: a single consolidated Business, multiple rows, or one primary row plus archived duplicates?

### M-5. Conflicting Seller-Supplied Data vs. Verified Data

**Possible scenario:** A merchant has carefully maintained contact and trade data on an unregistered Business, then that Business self-registers with different verified information.

**Questions to resolve:**

- Which fields are platform-owned and overwritten by verified onboarding data?  
- Which fields remain merchant-owned and must never be silently replaced?  
- If two merchants supplied different contact details for what becomes the same canonical Business, are those contacts global, per-relationship, or per-source?

### M-6. Merge Reversibility and Ops Visibility

**Possible scenario:** An auto-merge later proves wrong or a human needs to understand why two records were consolidated.

**Questions to resolve:**

- Is merge reversible by ops, or only compensatable through a second corrective merge?  
- What evidence should be stored and visible to support and admin teams: matched fields, source precedence, time of merge, initiating trigger?  
- When auto-merge is skipped because confidence is low, does the product require an explicit "possible duplicate" surface for operations?

---

### G-14. All-Businesses Directory Data Isolation Tension

**Where it appears:**

PRD 2, Section 10 "Non-Functional Requirements":

> "Data scoping: Counterparty records are scoped to the active business. Users who belong to multiple businesses have separate counterparty directories per business. No cross-business counterparty data leakage."

PRD 3, Section 6 "All-Businesses Directory," FR-D.2:

> "The directory also shows all counterparty records from across the platform."

The admin directory intentionally shows all Business records from all businesses — this is a deliberate exception for operational purposes. But it is in direct tension with the isolation guarantee in PRD 2\. The PRD does not acknowledge this exception explicitly or define what access controls govern who within the admin team can see which Business records. Given that Business records include contact details (email, phone) supplied by individual sellers, the admin visibility into those is a PDPL-relevant data access surface.

---

### G-15. Admin Role — Deactivation Between Peers Is Undefined

**Where it appears:**

Roles & Permissions PRD, Section 4.1:

> "Admin: Multiple Admins allowed. Can be designated as Authorized Signatory by the Owner."

The Roles PRD defines that Owner and Admin both have "Deactivate users" permission (Section 5 permission matrix). But it does not define whether an Admin can deactivate another Admin with equal or higher Authorized Signatory status, or whether only the Owner can remove other Admins. This would likely surface in any organisation with multiple Admin users.

---

## **Implementation Language in the PRDs**

Several passages across the Foundation PRDs cross the line from product requirements into technical implementation. A PRD should describe **what** the platform must do and **why** — outcomes, constraints and user-facing behaviour. How those outcomes are achieved (data model choices, field names, runtime enforcement strategy, async architecture) belongs in engineering design documents, not in PRDs.

The instances below are flagged not because the underlying intent is wrong — in most cases it is sound — but because expressing them in implementation terms creates a risk: engineering may treat the described mechanism as a constraint rather than an example, reducing design freedom unnecessarily.

---

### IP-1. Roles PRD — Section 2.2: Data Model Prescribed in Product Document

**Where it appears:**

Roles & Permissions PRD, Section 2.2 "Data Model — Build for Phase 2 from Day One":

> "The permission engine must be built to the Phase 2 data model from the first day of development, even though Phase 1 only exposes fixed role names. Roles are stored as entities with a permissions table. Platform-defined roles are pre-seeded with default permission sets."  
>   
> "Engineering must not hardcode role capabilities in application logic (e.g. if role \== 'Admin' then allow counterparty management). Role capabilities must always be resolved from the permissions table at runtime."  
>   
> "Phase 2 requires no data migration. The schema supports custom roles from day one. Phase 2 is a UI unlock, not a schema change."

**What belongs in the PRD:** The platform must support custom roles in Phase 2 without requiring a re-build of the permission engine. Phase 1 ships with fixed role names; Phase 2 adds merchant-defined custom roles. The permission model must accommodate this evolution.

**What does not:** Storage architecture ("permissions table," "entities"), runtime resolution strategy ("resolved from the permissions table at runtime") and migration constraints ("no data migration," "schema change") are engineering design decisions.

---

### IP-2. Roles PRD — Section 2.3: Internal Field and Model Names

**Where it appears:**

Roles & Permissions PRD, Section 2.3 "Authorized Signatory — Orthogonal to Role":

> "The Authorized Signatory is not a role. It is a boolean flag — is\_authorized\_signatory — on the MerchantMembership record."  
>   
> "The permission engine enforces this at the data layer, not only the UI layer."

**What belongs in the PRD:** The Authorized Signatory designation is orthogonal to role — any user of any role can be designated. The Owner's Authorized Signatory status is permanent and cannot be removed by any actor, including themselves. This must be enforced as a hard constraint, not only a UI guard.

**What does not:** The internal field name (`is_authorized_signatory`), the model name (`MerchantMembership`) and the enforcement layer ("data layer") are implementation choices.

---

### IP-3. Roles PRD — Section 10 NFR: Internal Field Names in Non-Functional Requirements

**Where it appears:**

Roles & Permissions PRD, Section 10 "Non-Functional Requirements":

> "Session integrity: active\_merchant\_id validated on every request. Cross-merchant data leakage via session manipulation prevented at the middleware layer."  
>   
> "Audit trail: Every permission-gated action logged with: user\_id, merchant\_id, membership\_id, action, timestamp, outcome. Authorized Signatory actions additionally log is\_authorized\_signatory state at time of action."  
>   
> "Admin containment: platform\_operator\_only permissions flagged in the permissions table. Permission engine rejects assignment of these to any non-platform-operator merchant role."  
>   
> "Owner signatory immutability: The Owner's is\_authorized\_signatory flag enforced as immutable at the data layer. No application-layer or UI path removes it."

**What belongs in the PRD:** Every request must be scoped to the active business context with no cross-business data leakage. All permission-gated actions must be logged with sufficient detail to reconstruct who did what and in what capacity. Platform-only permissions must be unassignable to merchant roles. The Owner's Authorized Signatory status must be permanently enforced.

**What does not:** `active_merchant_id`, `user_id`, `merchant_id`, `membership_id`, `is_authorized_signatory`, `platform_operator_only`, "middleware layer," "data layer," and "application-layer" are all implementation specifics.

---

### IP-4. Roles PRD — Section 2.1 and Section 4: Codebase and API Layer References

**Where it appears:**

Roles & Permissions PRD, Section 2.1 "One Unified Permission Engine":

> "This means one login screen, one session model, one audit trail and one codebase for permission enforcement."

Roles & Permissions PRD, Section 4 (pre-Owner window note):

> "The two Owner-exclusive actions (ownership transfer, account deletion) are enforced by hiding the CTAs in the UI and by a permission check at the API layer that verifies an active Owner membership record exists before permitting those actions."

**What belongs in the PRD:** Business users and Qawafel staff share a single permission model and audit trail. Ownership transfer and account deletion must be gated on the Owner role being active — not only hidden in the UI but rejected if attempted through any means.

**What does not:** "One codebase," "API layer," and "active Owner membership record" are implementation language. The product intent (hard enforcement, not soft hiding) is what matters.

---

### IP-5. PRD 2 — Section 10 NFR: Async Architecture and Atomicity Constraints

**Where it appears:**

PRD 2, Section 10 "Non-Functional Requirements":

> "Merge atomicity: The merge operation (record overwrite \+ badge update \+ linked account population) must be atomic. Partial merges that leave the record in an inconsistent state are not acceptable."  
>   
> "Background processing: Path B counterparty extraction and merge jobs run asynchronously. They must not block the invoice import response. Invoice import completes before counterparty processing finishes."

**What belongs in the PRD:** The merge must complete fully or not at all — a partial merge state must not be visible to any user. Invoice import completion must not be delayed by counterparty processing.

**What does not:** "Atomic" and "asynchronously" are engineering terms describing implementation strategies, not product outcomes. The PRD should state the observable behaviour; the implementation approach follows from that.

---

## **Summary of Priority**

The items above are not equally weighted. To make this easier for Product to respond to, they can be grouped into three buckets.

| Category | Items | Why this matters |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Must resolve before build | **C-4** TIN / VAT conflation, **C-5** non-taxable toggle direction, **C-6** Approve Business vs progressive unlock, **G-3** Path C quality label undefined, **G-4** ownership invitation new-user flow is TBD, **G-5** duplicate CR registration undefined, **G-8** VAT-registered declaration mechanism undefined, **G-13** merge overwrite vs gap-fill conflict, **M-1** through **M-6** merge/deduplication scenarios | These create direct implementation ambiguity, conflicting rules, or missing behaviour in critical flows. |
| Should clarify soon | **T-2** Path A vs Path B badge inconsistency, **T-5** tier-drop cascading effects, **T-8** IBAN validation vs admin action, **G-7** freelancer path coverage, **G-12** concurrent registration scenarios, **G-14** admin-directory data isolation exception, **G-15** admin-to-admin deactivation rules | These may not block the first pass, but they will produce inconsistent behaviour or rework if left open for too long. |
| Recommendations / future improvements | **C-2** terminology cleanup, **C-3** make the record model explicit, **T-1** clean-slate UX refinement, **T-3** confirm whether full submission before review is intentional, **T-6** business email concept, **T-7** in-session business switching, **T-9** auto-save persistence semantics, **G-1** duplicate FR-R.19, **G-2** version mismatch, **Implementation Language** section | These are still worth addressing, but they are either terminology quality, UX improvements, or document hygiene rather than immediate blockers. |
